synopsis: Evidence reuse across machine models is described as the biggest validation lever and the least documented: it must be designed in early, using common-core evidence plus explicit variant deltas rather than blanket family qualification [f366, f617, f12359]. No published case quantified cross-model time savings or demonstrated a heavy-machine family's validation shrinking from years to months; an under-four-month window therefore requires a narrower release claim or substantial evidence already in place [f261, f12361, f889]. Aerospace provides a qualified precedent: Lockheed Martin attributes F-35 Auto-GCAS integration in 2019, seven years earlier than planned, to agile development and reuse of F-16 work, while the booklet emphasizes decades of foundational development behind that acceleration [f1443, f1569]. Formal proven-in-use credit concerns a reused element with identical or highly similar definition and operating conditions, supported by sufficient service history; the booklet reports a 70% confidence basis for ISO 26262 and higher confidence under IEC 61508, but did not verify either route comprehensively [f12351, f7935, f7936, f7704, f15271]. Warning-system history can anchor encounter frequencies, detections, environmental distributions and operator behavior, but cannot validate the simulator or new closed-loop braking chain: adding braking changes the item, and warning-era records do not establish post-intervention outcomes [f12355, f12357, f7938, f11710]. Aviation guidance likewise permits relevant service history only with justified similarity and differences, while machine-family reuse requires explicit applicability arguments and configuration control covering sensors, tyres, brakes, payloads and software versions [f7925, f7045, f1141].

relations.note: Both identify cross-model reuse as the biggest lever and least documented.
Both make early design a condition for realizing reuse's product-family value.
Both report no published case quantifying cross-model reuse time savings.
Duplicate statements of the missing quantified time-saving case.
Both report vendor claims exceeding 10,000 mine-testing hours for an earlier generation.
Both report reuse enabling F-35 Auto-GCAS integration seven years early.
Both describe aerospace acceptance of service history subject to justified similarity.
The latter specifies applicant obligations and relevant attributes for service-history applicability.
Both condition tool-history confidence on similar versions, environments, maturity and usage.
Both state that proven-in-use evidence does not validate a simulator.
Both reject transferring warning-system history to braking because braking changes the item.
Both identify a 70 percent confidence basis for ISO 26262 proven-in-use.
Both say IEC 61508 demands higher confidence than the comparable ISO 26262 route.
The glossary adds sufficiently few failures to support the statistical service-history claim.
The glossary explains exposure uncertainty, censored outcomes and the unexercised braking chain.
Shared verified elements and variant-delta testing underpin the common-core-plus-deltas recommendation.
Configuration-dependent applicability explains why family evidence needs explicit justification.
Limited primary verification qualifies the glossary's categorical presentation of ISO clause requirements.
